name: Popular Music
subtitle: Battle of the Bands
blurb: This term we explore how Australian popular music uses rhythm, harmony and production to create style and identity. You will build your own track in GarageBand, and perform an Australian song of your choice.
question: How do the concepts of music shape the sound and style of popular music?
outcomes: uses performance skills to demonstrate understanding of the elements of music and communicate musical ideas
improvises, arranges or composes using the elements of music to create musical ideas
uses listening skills to describe music in relation to stylistic, cultural, historical or social contexts and the elements of music

assessment.name: Battle of the Bands
assessment.detail: A performance, solo or in a small group, and a GarageBand composition.

lessons.title: Welcome to Popular Music
lessons.intention: We are learning to identify characteristics of Australian popular genres.
criteria: I can describe at least two genre differences in Australian popular music.

rows: Distorted guitar riff, driving backbeat, live drum kit
Long synth pads, a slow build, deep sub bass under a live-sounding kit
Rapping in Yolŋu Matha and English, brass hook, trap hi-hats
A seven-year-old's voice over a family band, recorded at home rather than in a studio
Layered vocal harmony, polished production, tight groove

blocks.text: Baker Boy and Jessica Mauboy are First Nations artists. Listen for how each one uses music to say something about identity.

blocks.title: Your task
blocks.text: Choose the genre you connect with most. Write two sentences about what you notice in its instruments or production.
A category of music that shares common features - for example rock, pop or hip hop. Two songs in the same genre usually use similar instruments, grooves and production choices.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Word bank
blocks.text: Use these words: distorted, clean, programmed, acoustic, layered, punchy, smooth, heavy, bright, echoey, fast, slow. Sentence starter: “In this song I can hear … which makes it sound …”

Find an Australian artist who is not on this list. Identify their genre and describe two stylistic features that place them in it. Be ready to play a 30-second excerpt to the class and justify your choice.
What makes a song sound Australian to you?

lessons.title: Rhythm and Groove
lessons.intention: We are learning how groove shapes style in popular music.
criteria: I can explain how drum patterns create different feels across genres.

tracks.title: Backbeat - Jet, Are You Gonna Be My Girl

headers: Where the kick and snare land
rows: Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4
Sparse kick, snare or clap on 3, fast rolling hi-hats

blocks.title: Your task - Groove Comparison
blocks.text: Clap each groove as a class. Then on your worksheet, draw a simple icon for each groove, note the tempo, and describe the feel in your own words.

Beat - the steady pulse of the music. It is what you tap your foot to. Groove - the overall rhythmic feel created by the interaction of drums, bass and other instruments. Two songs can share a beat but have completely different grooves.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Clap it before you write it
blocks.text: Count “1 - 2 - 3 - 4” out loud and clap only on 2 and 4. That is a backbeat. Now clap on every number. That is four-on-the-floor. You have just played the difference between rock and dance music. For “describe the feel”, pick one: driving, bouncy, relaxed, heavy, floaty, urgent.

Transcribe one groove into simple notation on a four-beat grid, showing kick, snare and hi-hat on separate lines. Then compare the same groove across three Australian songs - does the tempo or the hi-hat pattern change the feel more?
Which groove is most iconic in Australian music, and why?

lessons.title: GarageBand Basics
lessons.intention: We are learning to set up a GarageBand project correctly.
criteria: I can create a new project, set the tempo, and enable the metronome.

blocks.brief: Getting started in GarageBand for iPad

blocks.title: Set up your project - follow along
items: Open GarageBand and choose Empty Project.
When asked to choose a track type, select Software Instrument.
Find the tempo in the display at the top of the window. Set it to 100 bpm.
Turn on the metronome. Press play and listen to the click.
Turn on the count-in so you get one bar of clicks before recording starts.
Save now: File → Save As. Name it Surname_PopularMusic and save to your student drive, not the desktop.

blocks.title: Save it properly, once
blocks.text: This is the project you build on all term and submit in Week 8. If it lives on the desktop of a shared machine, you will lose it.
A repeated musical phrase recorded and layered digitally. Most popular music is built from loops stacked on top of each other.

blocks.title: Stuck? Common problems
blocks.text: I can't hear the click. Check the metronome icon is highlighted, and that your headphones are plugged in properly. I can't find the tempo. It is the number in the display at the top centre. Click and drag it up or down. Nothing happens when I press record. Make sure a track is selected - it should be highlighted on the left.
Import a reference track of an Australian song you like. Work out its tempo by ear, then set your project tempo to match so the grid lines up with the song.
What tempo did you choose, and where did you save your project?

lessons.title: Recording and Programming Drums
lessons.intention: We are learning to record a drum part in GarageBand.
criteria: I can create a steady 8-bar beat in time.

blocks.brief: Programming a beat on the grid with the Beat Sequencer

blocks.title: Build an 8-bar drum loop
items: Add a Software Instrument track and choose a Drum Kit.
Decide which groove you are building - backbeat, four-on-the-floor, or trap. Write it down before you play.
Record kick and snare only for 8 bars. Ignore hi-hats for now.
Play it back. If it drifts, use quantise to snap the notes to the grid.
Record the hi-hats on a second pass, over the top.
Loop the region and check it still feels steady when it repeats.

blocks.title: This is assessment work.
blocks.text: The drum track you build today is the first layer of your Week 8 composition. Keep it.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Start simpler
blocks.text: Use a preset drum kit and program the beat by clicking notes onto the grid instead of playing it live. Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, and nothing else. That is a complete, correct rock groove. Remember which is which: kick is the low boom, snare is the sharp crack, hi-hat is the short metallic tick.
Add a drum fill every 4 bars so the loop has shape rather than just repeating. Then try the same groove on a different kit - acoustic against electronic - and describe what changes about the feel.
Which groove did you build, and did you program it or play it in?

lessons.title: Drums in Genres
lessons.intention: We are learning to compare rhythmic features across genres.
criteria: I can describe how grooves affect musical style.

tracks.title: Rock - Jet, Are You Gonna Be My Girl

blocks.title: Your task - Compare your loop to the real thing
blocks.text: Play your 8-bar loop from Lesson 4, then play a reference track in the same genre. Answer the questions below.

rows: What is different about the real track's drums?
Is the real track faster or slower than yours?
One change you will make to your loop

blocks.text: How many layers of sound are heard at once, and how they interact. A solo voice is a thin texture; a full band with backing vocals is a thick one.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Just compare two
blocks.text: Compare pop against rock only. Ask one question: are the drums played by a person or made by a computer? Then say which sounds heavier, and why you think so.

Groove carries cultural meaning as well as style. Choose an Australian song and argue how its groove contributes to the identity the artist is presenting. Does a pub rock backbeat say something different about Australia than a trap beat does?
Name one thing you will change about your drum loop next lesson.

blocks.title: Next:
blocks.text: Lessons 6-10 - Chords & Harmony. You will add a chord progression over the drum loop you just built.

lessons.title: Popular Chord Progressions
lessons.intention: We are learning how chords create harmony in popular songs.
criteria: I can play or sequence a simple chord progression.

blocks.call: Chord numerals are not chord names. They are seat numbers in a scale.
paras: Look down the table below and the same progression turns up twice, once as C - G - Am - F and once as G - D - Em - C. Different letters, same progression. That is the whole reason musicians write chords as numerals instead of letters: the numeral describes the shape, and the shape is what songs actually share. Two bands playing in different keys are playing the same four chords in the sense that matters.

Number the notes of a scale from one to seven. In C major that is C, D, E, F, G, A, B. A chord numeral tells you which of those notes the chord is built on, so I is the chord on note one, V is the chord on note five, and vi is the chord on note six. Change key and every letter moves, but the seats stay where they are.
The case of the numeral carries one more piece of information, and it is easy to miss.
A capital numeral is a major chord: I, IV and V.
A lowercase numeral is a minor chord: ii, iii and vi.

That is why the pop progression is written I-V-vi-IV rather than I-V-VI-IV. The third chord is the minor one, and it is the reason a progression built from three bright chords still has some shadow in it.

rows: The pop progression. Hundreds of songs use it
Rock and blues. Punchy and direct
Bad Moon Rising - Creedence Clearwater Revival
Almost the same three chords, but it falls home instead of climbing
Castle on the Hill - Ed Sheeran; Love Story - Taylor Swift (chorus)
Lifts early, then leans on the V to send you round again
blocks.heading: The progressions

tracks.title: I-V-IV - Bad Moon Rising, Creedence Clearwater Revival
I-IV-vi-V - Castle on the Hill, Ed Sheeran

blocks.title: Your task
blocks.text: Play I-V-vi-IV on keyboard or guitar as a whole-class jam, then practise it on your own instrument. Four beats per chord, round and round.
A sequence of chords that provides the harmony of a song. The same progression can appear in completely different genres - what changes is the instruments, tempo and production around it.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Start with two chords
blocks.text: Play just C and G, four beats each, swapping back and forth. That is a real progression and plenty of songs use only two chords. On keyboard, C major is the three white notes C-E-G played together. G major is G-B-D. Find them, hold them, and count four.
Try ii-V-I, or substitute a chord in I-V-vi-IV for one not in the table. What happens to the mood? Then work out the progression of a song you like by ear.
Why do you think so many pop songs use the same four chords?

lessons.title: Recording Chords in GarageBand
lessons.intention: We are learning to record a chord progression in GarageBand.
criteria: I can record a progression in time using a chosen instrument sound.

blocks.title: Record your chord track
items: Open your project. Your drum loop should already be there.
Add a new Software Instrument track. Choose a piano, electric piano or synth pad.
Set the loop to 8 bars so it matches your drums.
Record I-V-vi-IV, four beats per chord. That fills 4 bars, so play it twice.
Play it back with the drums. If the timing drifts, quantise.
Save.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Use Smart Instruments
blocks.text: Switch the track to Smart Piano or Smart Guitar. Tap a chord strip and it plays the whole chord in rhythm for you, in time. You choose the chords and when they change; GarageBand handles the fingers.
Layer two chord sounds - a pad underneath and a piano on top - so the harmony has depth. Or try inversions, keeping the top note the same as chords change, so the progression sounds smoother.
Play your chords to the person next to you. Do they sound pop, rock or EDM?

lessons.title: Harmony in Styles
lessons.intention: We are learning to identify how harmony changes across styles.
criteria: I can describe differences in how chords are used in at least two genres.

tracks.title: Piano ballad - Missy Higgins, Where I Stood
Pub rock - Jet, Are You Gonna Be My Girl
EDM pads - RÜFÜS DU SOL, Innerbloom

blocks.title: Your task - Listening chart
blocks.text: Listen to each excerpt and fill in the row. Type your answers straight into the chart.

headers: Do chords change fast or slow?

blocks.title: Need a hand? Just tick the box
blocks.text: Compare two styles only. For each one, tick: chords played by piano / guitar / synth. Chords change fast / slow. Mood is happy / sad / energetic / calm.
Compare harmonic rhythm - how often the chords change - across the three styles. Why might a ballad hold a chord for four bars while a rock song changes every bar? What does that do to the energy?
How would your progression sound played as EDM instead of rock?

lessons.title: Combining Drums and Chords
lessons.intention: We are learning to combine rhythm and harmony in GarageBand.
criteria: I can create a loop with chords and drums together.

blocks.brief: Recording more than one track and stacking them up

blocks.title: What lined up looks like
blocks.alt: Four bars of drum grid, one column per beat. The hi-hat plays on every beat, the kick on beats 1 and 3, the snare on beats 2 and 4. Above the drums, four chord blocks - C, G, A minor and F - each starting exactly on beat 1 of its own bar, so every chord change lands on a kick drum.
blocks.caption: Every chord change starts on beat 1 of a bar, on the same beat as a kick drum. If your chord region starts anywhere else, the two layers will drift apart as the loop repeats.

blocks.title: Lock the two layers together
items: Play your drums and chords together. Do the chord changes land on beat 1 of each bar?
If not, drag the chord region so it starts exactly on a bar line.
Check the balance - can you hear both, or is one drowning the other? Adjust the volume sliders.
Loop the 8 bars and listen three times through. It should feel steady, not rushed.
Save.

blocks.title: Checkpoint.
blocks.text: By the end of today you should have two working layers. Lessons 11-14 add bass and a riff on top of these.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Use a ready-made drum track
blocks.text: If your drum loop is not working, ask for the teacher drum track and layer your chords over that instead. The skill being practised today is combining layers, not rebuilding the drums.
Add a second 8-bar section with a different progression, so your track has contrast. Or vary the harmony the second time through - same chords, different voicing or rhythm.
Does your loop feel steady when it repeats? What did you fix?

lessons.title: Performance Preparation
lessons.intention: We are learning to rehearse and refine our chosen Australian song.
criteria: I can perform the first section of my song with accuracy.

blocks.title: Your song must be locked in today
blocks.text: It has to be by an Australian artist, and approved. If you have not chosen, do that first - rehearsal time is short and the performance is assessed in Lesson 19.

blocks.title: Solo or group - your choice.
blocks.text: You can perform on your own or in a small group. Both are worth the same marks. Pick whichever you will play your best in, and decide now, because it changes which song suits you.

blocks.title: Rehearsal plan
items: Play through the first section once, all the way, without stopping.
Find the hardest bar. Play just that bar, slowly, five times.
Play the bar before it and the bar after it, joined up.
Play the whole section again. It should be cleaner.
Write down what you will practise before next lesson.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Chorus only
blocks.text: Learn the chorus and nothing else. A chorus performed accurately and confidently is worth far more than a whole song played badly. Ask for a lyric sheet with the chords marked above the words.
Prepare a full verse and chorus, and accompany yourself - sing while playing, or add a backing part. Think about how you will start and finish, not just the middle.
What is the one bar you need to practise most, and why?

blocks.title: Next:
blocks.text: Lessons 11-15 - Bass & Hooks. You will add the bass line that ties your drums and chords together, then write the riff that makes the track yours.

lessons.title: The Role of Bass
lessons.intention: We are learning how the bass works in a pop rock band.
criteria: I can describe the main characteristics of the bass in a pop rock song.

blocks.heading: Bass in four pop rock songs

tracks.title: Jet - Are You Gonna Be My Girl
Tame Impala - The Less I Know The Better

blocks.title: Bass does two jobs at once.
blocks.text: It plays the lowest note of the harmony, so it tells your ear which chord you are on. And it locks to the kick drum, so it drives the rhythm. That is why a track feels empty without it.

blocks.title: Your task - What is the bass doing?
blocks.text: Listen to each song and describe the bass. Fill in at least three of the four rows.

headers: Does it follow the kick drum?

blocks.text: The low notes that support the harmony and rhythm of a song. Usually the lowest part you can hear, and usually the one you feel more than you notice.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Sentence starters
blocks.text: The bass is the low sound that holds the song up. Finish these: “In Jet, the bass …”    “In Tame Impala, the bass …”    “In Midnight Oil, the bass …” Useful words: deep, punchy, smooth, steady, moving, simple, loud.

All four are pop rock, so the differences are small and worth naming precisely. Compare how much the bass moves: one of these plays almost nothing but the root note of each chord, another has a bass line you could sing on its own. Explain what each choice does to the feel of the song.
Which of the four has the bass line you would most want to play, and what makes it good?

lessons.title: Recording Bass in GarageBand
lessons.intention: We are learning to record a bass line that works with chords and drums.
criteria: I can record a bass part that locks with the kick drum.

blocks.title: Record your bass track
items: Add a Software Instrument track and choose a bass sound.
Work out your root notes. For I-V-vi-IV in C, that is C - G - A - F.
Play one long note per chord to start. Four beats each.
Play it back with the drums. Does the bass land with the kick? That is the target.
Once it locks, try playing the root note on every beat instead of holding it.
Save.

blocks.text: The bass note is the letter the chord is named after. That is the rule, and it works for every chord in the table.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Use Smart Bass
blocks.text: Switch to Smart Bass and turn on autoplay. Choose a pattern, then tap the chord as it changes. GarageBand plays a bass line that already fits.
Add syncopated fills - notes that land off the beat - or write a walking bass line that steps between chords instead of jumping. Both make the bass a part people listen to rather than just feel.
Does your bass lock with the kick drum? How can you tell?

lessons.title: Hooks and Riffs
lessons.intention: We are learning the difference between a riff and a hook, and what makes each one stick.
criteria: I can explain the difference between a riff and a hook.
I can create a short riff or hook that repeats.

blocks.heading: Riffs and hooks in five songs

tracks.title: Hook in the lyrics - The Easybeats, Friday On My Mind
Riff on strings - The Veronicas, Untouched
Riff on flute, and the song's hook - Men At Work, Down Under
Riff on a xylophone sound - Gotye, Somebody That I Used To Know

blocks.call: Every riff can become a hook. Not every hook is a riff.
paras: A riff is a short instrumental pattern, usually two to four bars long, that repeats through a song. Three things make it a riff: it is short, it is played rather than sung, and it comes back. It is built from the notes of the chords underneath it, and it usually sits under or between the vocals rather than on top of them. The guitar figure that opens AC/DC's T.N.T. is a riff. It is under the singing for most of the song, and it is still the first thing you would play if someone asked you to play that song.

A hook is any part of a song written to catch the listener and stay in their head. It is named for the job it does, not for what plays it, so a hook can be sung, played, sampled or purely rhythmic. That is the real difference. A riff is described by what it is; a hook is described by what it achieves. A riff also repeats constantly, while a hook is often saved for the moment that matters most, usually the chorus, so that it lands instead of turning into wallpaper.
Hooks come in three kinds, and a song often runs more than one at once.
Melodic hook: a catchy tune, like the string line that drives The Veronicas' Untouched.
Rhythmic hook: a catchy pattern of long and short sounds, even on one note. The stomp-stomp-clap of Queen's We Will Rock You is a hook with no melody at all.
Lyrical hook: a catchy phrase, very often the song title. "Friday on my mind" lands at the end of the chorus every time.

The two overlap constantly, and that is not a fault in the words. When the riff is the most memorable thing in a song, the riff is also the hook. Down Under is the clearest case on this page: the flute figure is a riff by description, because it is short, played and repeated, and it is the hook by job, because it is the thing everyone remembers. What you cannot do is run it backwards. The sung title line in Gotye's chorus is a hook and it is not a riff, because it is sung and it does not repeat underneath the song the way a riff does.

What makes either one stick is the same short list: short enough to hold in your head, repeated often enough to learn, and simple enough to sing back after one hearing. Complicated ideas are rarely memorable. Notice that the five songs above carry their idea on five different things, guitar, voice, strings, flute and a xylophone sound. A hook is an idea, not an instrument.

blocks.heading: Riff or hook?
rows: Any part written to catch your ear
Three notes to a whole chorus
Played, sung, sampled or just a rhythm
Over and over, often right through
Saved for the moment it matters most
Out the front, usually the chorus
Flute figure, Men At Work, Down Under
Title line, The Easybeats, Friday On My Mind

blocks.title: In your book
items: Rule up two columns, Riff and Hook. Copy the definition of each one from the liner notes above, in full sentences.
Under each definition, write the three things that make it what it is. For a riff: short, played, repeated. For a hook: catchy, memorable, and named for its job rather than its instrument.
List the three kinds of hook, with the example song for each.
Write one sentence explaining the overlap: when is a riff also the hook?
Choose two of the five songs above. For each, name whether you are describing a riff or a hook, and give one reason from your definitions.
You need both definitions again in Lesson 15 and in the key words check in Lesson 25, so write them properly now.

blocks.title: Your task - Design your riff
blocks.text: Before you touch GarageBand, plan it. Use three or four notes only. Sing or hum it first - if you cannot sing it, it is too complicated.

rows: Where will it appear in the track?

blocks.text: A short instrumental pattern, usually two to four bars, that repeats through a song. Played rather than sung, most often on guitar, bass, keys or synth, and it usually sits under or between the vocals.

Any part of a song written to catch the listener and stay in their head. A hook is named for its job, not for what plays it, so it can be melodic, rhythmic or lyrical, and sung, played or sampled. When a riff is the most memorable thing in a song, the riff is also the hook.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Use the three-note model
blocks.text: Start from the teacher's three-note riff and change one thing - a note, the rhythm, or the instrument sound. That is still your riff, and it will work over your chords. Safe notes over a C-G-Am-F progression: C, E, G, A. Any of them will sound right.
Take your riff and flip it into another genre - play a rock guitar riff as an EDM synth line, or a synth hook on distorted guitar. Same notes, different world. What has to change besides the sound?
Sing your riff to the person next to you. Can they sing it back?

lessons.title: Recording Your Riff
lessons.intention: We are learning to record a riff that gives identity to our composition.
criteria: I can record a riff that repeats in time and fits with my other parts.
I can explain what quantise does to a recording.

blocks.brief: Recording a riff on the virtual guitars

blocks.call: A riff has to survive fifty repeats. That is a very different job from playing something once.
paras: This is the fourth and last of the required layers, and it is the one a listener hears most often. At a typical pop tempo of 120 beats per minute, a two-bar riff running through a three-minute track repeats about forty-five times. Anything slightly annoying on the first repeat is unbearable by the fortieth. That is why the plan in Lesson 13 asked for three or four notes. The fewer moving parts a riff has, the longer it survives.

Quantise means snapping the notes you played onto the nearest line of the beat grid. It does not change which notes you played or how hard you hit them, only when each one starts, so a take with the right feel and loose timing can be rescued instead of rerecorded. Set the quantise value to match the fastest note in your riff. If your riff moves in eighth notes, quantise to 1/8. Quantise that same riff to 1/4 and half your notes get dragged onto beats they were never meant to land on.

Once one take is right, stop playing it. Tap the region, choose Loop, and GarageBand repeats it for you for as far as you drag it. Copying a take that is right is not cheating. It is how nearly every record you listen to is made, and one loop that is exactly in time beats eight live takes that are nearly in time.

If you can hear your riff on its own but it vanishes once all four layers are playing, the problem is almost never volume. It is register, meaning how high or low the part sits. Your bass is at the bottom, your chords fill the middle, and a riff written in the middle of that is fighting the chords for the same space. Move the riff up an octave and it will appear without you touching a single fader. Turn it up only if moving it did not work.

Repetition is what makes a riff memorable and it is also what makes a track boring, which sounds like a contradiction and is not. The professional fix is variation, not novelty. Keep the shape and change one thing: shift the rhythm, alter one note, or drop the riff out altogether for four bars. Bringing something back only works if you took it away.

blocks.title: Record your riff
items: Add a track and choose the sound you planned in Lesson 13.
Record your riff over the top of drums, chords and bass.
Quantise if the timing is loose.
Copy the region so the riff repeats across the loop.
Listen to all four layers together. Can you still hear the riff, or is it buried? Adjust the volume.
Save.

blocks.text: Snapping recorded notes onto the nearest line of the beat grid so that loose timing becomes exact. It changes when a note starts, not which note it is or how loud it is. Quantise to the value of the fastest note in the part.

blocks.title: In your book
items: Quantise: copy the definition from the key word box, in a full sentence.
Work out how many times your own riff will repeat. Take the length of your track in bars and divide it by the length of your riff in bars. Write the number down.
Copy the rule for a buried riff: if you cannot hear it, change its register before you change its volume.
Name the one thing you will vary in the second half of your track, and say what that change will do to the listener.

blocks.title: You now have all four required layers
blocks.text: drums, chords, bass and riff. Lessons 16-18 are about shaping them into a finished track.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Record it one note at a time
blocks.text: You do not have to play it live. Draw the notes onto the grid one at a time, in the piano roll. The result sounds identical and you control exactly where each note lands.

Write a variation of your riff for the second half of the track - same shape, one or two notes changed, or the rhythm displaced. Then try dropping the riff out entirely for four bars before it returns, and listen to what its absence does.
Which of your four layers is the most interesting to listen to, and why?

lessons.title: Performance Check-In
lessons.intention: We are learning to rehearse and refine our performance for assessment.
criteria: I can perform an excerpt of my song with accuracy, stylistic awareness and expression.
I can give feedback that names which of the three it is about.

blocks.title: Your task
blocks.text: Perform 30 to 60 seconds of your chosen Australian song for the class. This is a rehearsal, not the assessment - the point is to find out what still needs work while there is time to fix it.

blocks.title: Audience job.
blocks.text: Listen properly, then give one thing that worked and one thing to work on. Name which of the three you are talking about. "The timing in the chorus was solid" is accuracy, and it is useful. "It was good" names nothing and helps nobody.

blocks.call: You are not marked on how hard the song is. You are marked on three things, and a simple song can meet all three.
paras: Lesson 19 is the assessment and this lesson is the rehearsal for it, so today is the last cheap chance to find out what is not working. The rubric has three parts and they are marked separately, which means a performance can be strong in one and weak in another. Knowing which is which is what turns practising into improving.

Accuracy is the mechanical part: the right notes, the right rhythm, and a tempo that does not creep up. It is the easiest of the three to fix, because the fix is always the same one. Slow the passage down until you can play it perfectly, then bring the speed back up a little at a time.

Stylistic awareness is whether it sounds like the genre it came from. The same four chords played as a clean strum, a distorted riff or a soft arpeggio are three different styles, and only one of them is your song. Go back to the recording and copy how the original attacks the notes, not only which notes it plays.

Expression is what you do on top of correct: getting louder into the chorus, easing off in the verse, holding the last note instead of clipping it. It is the part students skip because it is not written in the notes, and it is the part that most changes how a performance lands on an audience.

None of the three needs a difficult song. A shortened, simplified version played accurately, in style and with dynamics marks better than an ambitious version played nervously. Pick the version you can actually perform, then make that one good.

blocks.heading: What you are marked on
headers: What it sounds like when it is missing
rows: Right notes, right rhythm, steady tempo
Wrong notes, or the tempo creeping up as you get nervous
It sounds like the genre it came from
Correct, but flat and generic. It could be any song
Dynamics and phrasing, not only correct notes
Every bar at the same volume from the first to the last

blocks.title: In your book
items: Fill in the four key words above from memory first. Only then go back to the lesson listed beside each one and correct what you had.
Copy the three things you are marked on, with a one-line definition of each in your own words.
Write down the feedback you were given today, and name which of the three it belongs to.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Play the chorus only
blocks.text: A simplified section, played accurately, is a real performance. Use your annotated lyric and chord sheet, and play the part you know best.
Perform an extended section, and add accompaniment or a backing part. Think about stagecraft too - how you start, how you finish, and what you do if you make a mistake mid-song.
What is the single thing you will improve before the assessment?

blocks.title: Next:
blocks.text: Lessons 16-20 - Texture, Effects & Assessment. You will finish the track and both assessments happen.

lessons.title: Texture and Layering
lessons.intention: We are learning to use texture to build density in music.
criteria: I can add multiple layers to create contrast in my track.

blocks.title: Contrast is the point.
blocks.text: A track where everything plays all the time is exhausting. Take layers away in the verse and add them in the chorus, and the chorus feels bigger without being louder.

blocks.title: Add a layer
items: Choose one new layer: a pad, a countermelody, or extra percussion.
Record it over your existing four layers.
Now mute one layer for the first 8 bars and unmute it after. Listen to the difference.
Decide which layers belong in your quiet section and which in your loud one.
Save.

blocks.text: Also called timbre. The unique sound quality of an instrument, voice or electronic effect. It is what makes a piano and a guitar sound different playing the same note.
How loud or soft the music is, and how that changes across a song. Adding layers can make a section feel bigger without turning anything up.

blocks.title: Need a hand? One layer is enough
blocks.text: Add a single pad sound holding one long chord underneath everything. That is a real texture layer and it will make your track sound fuller straight away. Thin texture means few layers, like one voice and a guitar. Thick means many, like a full band with backing vocals.
Try polyphonic layering - two independent melodies running at once that both work on their own and together. Harder than it sounds, and it is what separates a stack of loops from an arrangement.
How many layers does your track have now, and which one would you remove first?

lessons.title: Effects
lessons.intention: We are learning to apply effects to shape sound in a composition.
criteria: I can use at least two effects to change timbre in my track.

blocks.brief: Applying effects: EQ, reverb, echo and compression

rows: Makes a sound feel like it is in a space - room, hall, stadium
Repeats the sound like an echo
Adjusts frequencies (bass, middle, treble) to shape the sound
Removes high or low frequencies, often swept for build-ups

blocks.title: Your task
blocks.text: Apply at least two effects to parts of your composition. Listen before and after each one so you can hear what it actually changed.

blocks.title: Less is more
blocks.text: Reverb on everything turns a track to mush. Pick one or two parts that need it and leave the rest dry.
EQ - adjusting frequencies (bass, middle, treble) to shape sound. Reverb - an effect that makes a sound feel like it is in a space, for example a room, hall or stadium.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Use a preset
blocks.text: Ask for the preset effect chains. Pick one, apply it to a track, and listen to what changed. You still meet the criteria - the skill is hearing the difference, not building the chain from scratch.

Automate an effect so it changes over time - a filter sweep building into a chorus, or a reverb throw on the last word of a phrase. Automation is what makes a track sound produced rather than assembled.
Which two effects did you use, and on which tracks?

lessons.title: Structure and Arrangement
lessons.intention: We are learning to organise songs into clear sections.
criteria: I can structure my track using contrasting sections.

blocks.brief: Powderfinger, My Happiness - listen for where each section starts, and what drops out at the start of each verse

blocks.title: Build your arrangement
items: Turn on arrangement markers in GarageBand.
Label your sections: Intro, Verse, Chorus, Bridge, Outro.
Make at least two contrasting sections - they must differ in which layers play, not just repeat.
Strip the intro back. Drums alone, or riff alone, is a strong opening.
Play it start to finish. Does it go somewhere, or just repeat?
Save.

blocks.text: The arrangement of sections in a piece of music, and the order they come in. In most pop and rock songs that is some combination of intro, verse, chorus, bridge and outro.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Use an A-B structure
blocks.text: Two sections is all you need. A = quieter, fewer layers. B = everything playing. Then A again. That is a complete, correct structure.
Build a full verse-chorus-bridge-outro form. Analyse an Australian song you like, map its structure bar by bar, then replicate that shape with your own material.
How many sections does your track have, and how are they different from each other?

lessons.title: Solo or Group Performance
lessons.intention: We are learning to perform music with accuracy and style.
criteria: I can perform a piece that shows expressive and stylistic qualities.

blocks.title: This lesson is assessed.
blocks.text: You perform your chosen Australian popular song as a soloist or in a small ensemble. Marked against the rubric.

blocks.title: What you are marked on
items: Accuracy - right notes, right rhythm, steady tempo
Stylistic awareness - does it sound like the genre it comes from?
Expression - dynamics and phrasing, not just correct notes

blocks.title: Audience.
blocks.text: Respectful listening is part of the lesson. No talking, no phones, and applaud everyone.

blocks.title: Adjustments available
blocks.text: A shortened performance, or a simplified version of the song, is a valid submission. Annotated lyric and chord sheets are available. Speak to your teacher before the lesson if you need either.

blocks.title: Going further
blocks.text: Perform an extended arrangement, include live accompaniment, or bring in a backing track you have made yourself.

lessons.title: GarageBand Composition
lessons.intention: We are learning to create and present an original composition in popular style.
criteria: I can submit a completed track with drums, chords, bass, riff and effects.

blocks.title: Submit two files.
blocks.text: An audio export (so it can be played) and the .band project file (so your work on the layers can be seen). Missing either one is an incomplete submission.

blocks.title: Submission checklist - tick every row before you submit
blocks.text: Submission checklist - tick every row before you submit

rows: Drum track, steady and in time
Bass line that locks with the kick

blocks.title: Adjustments available
blocks.text: A shorter track of 30 to 45 seconds with fewer layers is a valid submission. Work through the checklist above with your teacher before you upload.

blocks.title: Going further
blocks.text: Extend the track with additional sections, use advanced automation, or record live instruments or vocals and mix them in with your programmed parts.

blocks.title: Next:
blocks.text: Lessons 21-25 - Showcase & Reflection. You will hear everyone's tracks and look back at what Australian popular music is actually saying.

lessons.title: Showcase Listening Session
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate compositions using the concepts of music.
criteria: I can describe how texture, timbre and dynamics are used in a peer's track.

blocks.title: Your task
blocks.text: Everyone plays their track. For each one you hear, note how the composer used the concepts of music. Use the proper vocabulary - that is the skill being practised.

blocks.title: Feedback rule.
blocks.text: Everyone in this room made something from nothing. Comment on the music, not the person, and find something real to praise before you suggest a change.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Sentence starters
blocks.text: “I liked the use of …”    “The texture was thick or thin because …”    “The loudest part was …” Listen to one or two tracks closely rather than trying to cover everyone.
Lead the feedback discussion for a track. Identify specific production techniques the composer used - not just what you heard, but how you think they made it happen.
Which track sounded most different from yours, and what did they do that you did not?

lessons.title: Reflecting on Australian Popular Music
lessons.intention: We are learning to reflect on the cultural identity expressed through Australian popular music.
criteria: I can identify features that make Australian popular music unique.

blocks.title: Back where we started.
blocks.text: You met these artists in Lesson 1 and listened for instruments and production. Now you have made a track yourself, listen again for something harder: what are they using music to say?

blocks.title: Your task - The Australian sound
blocks.text: Brainstorm what makes Australian popular music distinctive. Think about language, accent, subject matter, instruments, and the stories artists choose to tell.

headers: What is distinctly Australian about their music?

blocks.text: Baker Boy raps in Yolŋu Matha as well as English. That is a deliberate choice about identity, made in a genre that came from somewhere else entirely. Miles Phillips wrote Eastern Rosellas when he was seven, about birds at his grandparents' place, recorded it at home with his dad on drums, and went in at number five on the ARIA chart - the youngest Australian ever to chart.

blocks.title: Need a hand? One artist, one feature
blocks.text: Choose the artist you like most and name a single thing that makes their music sound Australian. One clear idea is enough.
Australian artists work in genres that began overseas - hip hop, rock, EDM. Explain how they fuse those global forms with something local, and what that fusion achieves culturally.
Has your answer to "what makes a song sound Australian" changed since Lesson 1?

lessons.title: Comparative Listening
lessons.intention: We are learning to compare how the concepts of music shape genre.
criteria: I can explain at least two similarities and two differences between artists.

tracks.title: Artist B - RÜFÜS DU SOL, Innerbloom

blocks.title: Your task
blocks.text: Compare two Australian artists from different genres - AC/DC against RÜFÜS DU SOL, for example. Find two things they share and two ways they differ.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Sentence frames
blocks.text: “Both artists …”    “A uses … but B uses …”    “The biggest difference is …” Fill in two rows rather than all four, and work through it with your teacher.

One of these bands plays rock instruments straight to tape; the other builds tracks from synths and programmed parts and then has to work out how to play them live. Explain how the technology shapes what each band can do, on the record and on stage.
Which of the two artists is closer to the track you made, and why?

lessons.title: Extension Workshop
lessons.intention: We are learning to extend our skills through self-directed projects.
criteria: I can independently apply new ideas to expand my music-making.

blocks.title: Choose one pathway
blocks.text: Choose one pathway

rows: Take your track and rebuild it in a different genre. Same riff, new world
Learn a new Australian song, or extend the one you performed in Lesson 19
Go back into your composition and improve it using techniques you have since learnt

blocks.title: Need a hand? Remix a short section
blocks.text: Take one loop from your track and change the instrument sounds and the tempo. That is a remix, and it is a genuine creative decision.
Set your own brief and direction. Advanced production, genre fusion, or recording live players are all open. Decide what you want to have made by the end of the lesson, then make it.
Which pathway did you choose, and what did you learn from it?

lessons.title: Wrap-Up and Reflection
lessons.intention: We are learning to reflect on our growth and identify future goals in music.
criteria: I can describe what I improved in and set a target for future learning.

blocks.title: Your reflection
blocks.text: Look back over the whole term. In Lesson 1 you had never opened this project; by Lesson 20 you had written and produced a track and performed a song in front of people.

rows: What did I improve most in this term?
What was hardest, and how did I get past it?
Performing or composing - which suited me better?

blocks.title: Playback session.
blocks.text: We finish by listening to the tracks again, properly, as an audience rather than as markers.

blocks.title: Need a hand? Reflection starters
blocks.text: “One thing I did well was …”    “I found it hard when …”    “Next term I want to …” You can answer these out loud instead of writing them.
Evaluate your development critically. Where is the ceiling on your current skills, what specifically would you need to learn to get past it, and what is an ambitious but real goal for next term?

blocks.title: Next term:
blocks.text: Film and Video Game Music. You will use the same GarageBand skills to score picture - writing music that has to fit something happening on screen.
